record.target: Why should your preferred duty take priority over the competing rescue or fidelity claim?
record.reply: Within Kantian deontology the promise to Cara generates a perfect duty of fidelity. A perfect duty forbids the contradictory opposite (making a promise one intends to break); universalising that maxim would destroy the institution of promising. The rescue of Ben is an imperfect duty of beneficence because Ada has no special tie to Ben beyond general concern for others. Imperfect duties admit latitude; they obligate adopting some maxims of aid, not every possible specific aid. When two duties conflict, Kant holds that perfect duties set strict constraints on maxims that imperfect duties cannot override. Therefore, breaking the promise is categorically impermissible, whereas failing this particular rescue is a permissible (though regrettable) omission consistent with still adopting other beneficent maxims.
record.framework_commitment: Kant: perfect duties (e.g., fidelity) have priority over imperfect duties (e.g., beneficence).
record.reasoning_bridge: Classify promise-keeping as perfect duty; classify rescuing stranger as imperfect beneficence; apply Kantian hierarchy to resolve conflict.
record.remaining_uncertainty: Whether life-threatening stakes can elevate beneficence here to a perfect positive duty of rescue; whether the promise was valid given resource scarcity.
record.reversal_condition: If Ben’s rescue constituted a perfect positive duty (e.g., special obligation or universally necessary aid), or if the promise was invalid, then duty priority could reverse.
